newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank says dlr had corrected at 1.65 marks.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank says dlr had corrected at 1.65 marks.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Wednesday acted to counter a sharp rise in the U.S. dollar against the mark, knocking down a report from U.S. news agency MNSI that said Germany was keen to see a further rise in the dollar.

Chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber, in an official statement from the central bank, said the Bundesbank continued to support a statement made by the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations at a meeting in Berlin this past weekend.
"That statement said the dollar has been corrected, and it was made at a rate of 1.65 marks," he said. The dollar surged to about 1.69 marks on Wednesday morning after the MNSI report.
The dollar fell to as low as 1.6750 marks in an immediate response to the Bundesbank statement on Wednesday morning.
"The opinion expressed in the MNSI report does not exist within the Bundesbank," Koerber said.
"The Bundesbank firmly backs the Berlin statement. The Bundesbank is definitively not of the opinion that the dollar should rise further," he added.

This past weekend, G7 finance ministers and central bank governors said the misalignment in the dollar seen when it fell to a record low in 1995 had been corrected, and they did not want to see excessive market volatility.
But Market News Service, quoting sources close to the German finance ministry, reported late on Tuesday from Washington that Germany was seeking a dollar between 1.70 marks and 1.75 marks.

The Bundesbank spokesman also noted that U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin had again repeated his view that although the U.S. was interested in a strong dollar, the dollar had now been strong for some time.
This statement, first made on Friday evening, was seen by markets as a subtle change in the U.S. position. The administration had in the past repeatedly called for a strong dollar.
